claim: JC polyomavirus (JCPyV) is a prevalent member of the human virome.
source: JC polyomavirus (JCPyV) is a prevalent member of the human virome (Kamminga et al., 2018; Viscidi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kamminga et al., 2018 and Viscidi et al., 2011

claim: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a fatal demyelinating brain disease caused by JCPyV.
source: Immunological perturbations are a necessary antecedent for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a fatal demyelinating brain disease caused by JCPyV (Haley and Atwood, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haley and Atwood, 2017

claim: PML was originally described as a rare complication of hematological malignancies.
source: PML was originally described as a rare complication of hematological malignancies and its incidence dramatically increased in the pre-HAART AIDS epoch (Astrom et al., 1958; Berger et al., 1987; Krupp et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Astrom et al., 1958; Berger et al., 1987; Krupp et al., 1985

claim: PML incidence dramatically increased in the pre-HAART AIDS epoch.
source: PML was originally described as a rare complication of hematological malignancies and its incidence dramatically increased in the pre-HAART AIDS epoch (Astrom et al., 1958; Berger et al., 1987; Krupp et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Astrom et al., 1958; Berger et al., 1987; Krupp et al., 1985

claim: PML has re-emerged as a complication of immunomodulatory therapies including natalizumab for relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
source: PML has 're-emerged' as a complication of immunomodulatory therapies, such as natalizumab (α4 integrin humanized mAb) for treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), rituximab (CD20 humanized mAb) for chronic lymphocytic leukemia and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, and efalizumab (LFA-1 humanized mAb) for severe plaque psoriasis (Carson et al., 2009; Kleinschmidt-DeMasters and Tyler, 2005; Kothary et al., 2011; Langer-Gould et al., 2005; Schwab et al., 2012; Van Assche et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Carson et al., 2009; Kleinschmidt-DeMasters and Tyler, 2005; Kothary et al., 2011; Langer-Gould et al., 2005; Schwab et al., 2012; Van Assche et al., 2005

claim: JCPyV isolates from PML patients contain unique mutations not found in virus present in patients' urine or in circulating archetype strains.
source: JCPyV isolates from the brains, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and blood of PML patients contain unique mutations not found in virus present in patients' urine or in circulating (archetype) strains (Van Loy et al., 2015; Vaz et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Van Loy et al., 2015; Vaz et al., 2000

claim: JCPyV-PML variants contain rearrangements in the noncoding control region (NCCR) including deletions, insertions, and duplications.
source: These JCPyV-PML variants contain rearrangements in the noncoding control region (NCCR) including deletions, insertions, and duplications.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript text

claim: NCCR rearrangements alter transcription factor binding sites and enhance viral replication in glial cells.
source: These rearrangements alter transcription factor binding sites and enhance viral replication in glial cells (Gosert et al., 2010; Marshall et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gosert et al., 2010; Marshall et al., 2010

claim: Most JCPyV-PML variants have non-synonymous mutations in VP1, the major viral capsid protein.
source: In addition, most JCPyV-PML variants have non-synonymous mutations in VP1, the major viral capsid protein, with the most common being a leucine-to-phenylalanine substitution at residue 54 (L54F) and a serine-to-phenylalanine/tyrosine substitution at residue 268 (S268F/Y) (Gorelik et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gorelik et al., 2011

claim: The most common VP1 mutations in JCPyV-PML are L54F and S268F/Y.
source: In addition, most JCPyV-PML variants have non-synonymous mutations in VP1, the major viral capsid protein, with the most common being a leucine-to-phenylalanine substitution at residue 54 (L54F) and a serine-to-phenylalanine/tyrosine substitution at residue 268 (S268F/Y) (Gorelik et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gorelik et al., 2011

claim: VP1 mutations have been reported to alter viral receptor binding, resulting in the utilization of a restricted set of receptors for cellular attachment and entry.
source: These VP1 mutations have been reported to alter viral receptor binding, resulting in the utilization of a restricted set of receptors for cellular attachment and entry, thereby altering viral tropism (Geoghegan et al., 2017; Maginnis et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Geoghegan et al., 2017; Maginnis et al., 2013

claim: In hypomyelinated RAG–/– mice engrafted with human glial precursor cells, infection with wild type or VP1 mutant JCPyVs resulted in similar levels of glial cell infection.
source: In hypomyelinated RAG–/– mice engrafted with human glial precursor cells (GPCs), however, infection with wild type or VP1 mutant JCPyVs resulted in similar levels of glial cell infection (Kondo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kondo et al., 2014

claim: PML patient sera only weakly neutralized patient-matched JCPyV VP1 variants.
source: PML patient sera only weakly neutralized patient-matched JCPyV VP1 variants (Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ray et al., 2015

claim: Mouse polyomavirus (MuPyV) shares many features with JCPyV, including asymptomatic persistent infection, viral persistence in the kidney, and control by the virus-specific adaptive immune response.
source: Mouse polyomavirus (MuPyV) shares many features with JCPyV, including asymptomatic persistent infection, viral persistence in the kidney, and control by the virus-specific adaptive immune response (Berger et al., 2017; Du Pasquier et al., 2004; Han Lee et al., 2006; Szomolanyi-Tsuda and Welsh, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berger et al., 2017; Du Pasquier et al., 2004; Han Lee et al., 2006; Szomolanyi-Tsuda and Welsh, 1996

claim: MuPyV and JCPyV are non-enveloped, circular dsDNA viruses with capsids ~45 nm in diameter.
source: MuPyV and JCPyV are non-enveloped, circular dsDNA viruses with capsids ~45 nm in diameter.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript text

claim: MuPyV and JCPyV have 5 kb genomes that encode the nonstructural T antigen proteins and the VP1 and VP2/VP3 structural proteins.
source: Their 5 kb genomes encode the nonstructural T antigen proteins and the VP1 and VP2/VP3 structural proteins.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript text

claim: Five copies of VP1 intertwine to form each capsomer subunit that also incorporates one copy of VP2/VP3.
source: Five copies of VP1 intertwine to form each capsomer subunit that also incorporates one copy of VP2/VP3 (Hurdiss et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hurdiss et al., 2016

claim: The core secondary structure formed by VP1 is the antiparallel β barrel structure commonly called the jellyroll.
source: The core secondary structure formed by VP1 is the antiparallel β barrel structure commonly called the jellyroll.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript text

claim: The X-ray structure of MuPyV VP1 pentamers has been solved at resolutions ranging from 1.64 Å to 2.0 Å.
source: The X-ray structure of MuPyV VP1 pentamers has been solved at resolutions ranging from 1.64 Å to 2.0 Å (Buch et al., 2015; Stehle and Harrison, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buch et al., 2015; Stehle and Harrison, 1997

claim: There is a 3.65 Å resolution X-ray map for MuPyV icosahedral capsid.
source: There are several structures of the entire icosahedral capsid including a 3.65 Å resolution X-ray map for MuPyV and a 3.4 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of BKPyV (Hurdiss et al., 2018; Stehle and Harrison, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hurdiss et al., 2018; Stehle and Harrison, 1996

claim: There is a 3.4 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of BKPyV icosahedral capsid.
source: There are several structures of the entire icosahedral capsid including a 3.65 Å resolution X-ray map for MuPyV and a 3.4 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of BKPyV (Hurdiss et al., 2018; Stehle and Harrison, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hurdiss et al., 2018; Stehle and Harrison, 1996

claim: A 4.2 Å map of BKPyV interacting with single chain variable fragment (scFv) provided insight into antibody neutralization of polyomavirus.
source: Notably, a 4.2 Å map of BKPyV interacting with single chain variable fragment (scFv) provided insight into antibody neutralization of polyomavirus (Lindner et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindner et al., 2019

claim: S268 of JCPyV corresponds to V296 of MuPyV VP1, with the residues mapping to the same position on the capsid.
source: S268 of JCPyV corresponds to V296 of MuPyV VP1, with the residues mapping to the same position on the capsid (Sunyaev et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sunyaev et al., 2009

claim: MuPyV carrying the V296F VP1 mutation was impaired in its ability to replicate in the kidney.
source: We found that MuPyV carrying the V296F VP1 mutation was impaired in its ability to replicate in the kidney, but replicated in the brain equivalently to parental virus.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the manuscript text

claim: MuPyV carrying the V296F VP1 mutation replicated in the brain equivalently to parental virus.
source: We found that MuPyV carrying the V296F VP1 mutation was impaired in its ability to replicate in the kidney, but replicated in the brain equivalently to parental virus.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the manuscript text

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the MuPyV:Fab complex was resolved to 3.2 Å resolution.
source: Using cryo-EM and a custom sub-particle refinement approach, we resolved an MuPyV:Fab complex map to 3.2 Å resolution.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the manuscript text

claim: Compared to mice inoculated subcutaneously with parental A2, mice given A2.V296F showed significantly lower infection levels in the kidney 4 days post-infection.
source: Compared to mice inoculated subcutaneously (s.c.) with parental A2, mice given A2.V296F showed significantly lower infection levels in the kidney 4 days post-infection (dpi) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: A2 virus-infected mice developed large, numerous VP1+ foci in the kidney at day 7 post-infection.
source: A2 virus-infected mice developed large, numerous VP1+ foci in the kidney, but A2.V296F-infected mice exhibited only small, sporadic VP1+ foci (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: A2.V296F-infected mice exhibited only small, sporadic VP1+ foci in the kidney at day 7 post-infection.
source: A2 virus-infected mice developed large, numerous VP1+ foci in the kidney, but A2.V296F-infected mice exhibited only small, sporadic VP1+ foci (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: At four days post-infection following intracranial inoculation, A2.V296F showed equivalent infection in the brain to A2.
source: At four dpi following i.c. inoculation, A2.V296F showed equivalent infection in the brain to A2 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Infection with either A2 or A2.V296F resulted in sporadic VP1+ ependymal cells or astrocytes in the brain.
source: Infection with either virus resulted in sporadic VP1+ ependymal cells (vimentin+) or astrocytes (GFAP+) (Figure 1E; Lavado and Oliver, 2011; Tissir et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citations to Lavado and Oliver, 2011; Tissir et al., 2010

claim: In mice infected subcutaneously with a 1:1 mixture of A2 and A2.V296F, a reduced A2.V296F:A2 ratio was seen in both the kidney and bone marrow at 14 days post-infection.
source: In mice infected s.c. a reduced A2.V296F:A2 ratio was seen in both the kidney and bone marrow, but this ratio was significantly higher and nearly equal in the brain (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: In mice infected subcutaneously with a 1:1 mixture of A2 and A2.V296F, the A2.V296F:A2 ratio was significantly higher and nearly equal in the brain at 14 days post-infection.
source: In mice infected s.c. a reduced A2.V296F:A2 ratio was seen in both the kidney and bone marrow, but this ratio was significantly higher and nearly equal in the brain (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: In intracranially inoculated mice, A2.V296F infected the brain 1:1 with A2 at 14 days post-infection.
source: In i.c. inoculated mice A2.V296F infected the brain 1:1 with A2, but in the kidney was significantly outcompeted by A2, resulting in >1:100 A2.V296F:A2 ratio in the kidneys of some mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: In intracranially inoculated mice, A2.V296F was significantly outcompeted by A2 in the kidney, resulting in >1:100 A2.V296F:A2 ratio in the kidneys of some mice at 14 days post-infection.
source: In i.c. inoculated mice A2.V296F infected the brain 1:1 with A2, but in the kidney was significantly outcompeted by A2, resulting in >1:100 A2.V296F:A2 ratio in the kidneys of some mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Infection with either A2 or A2.V296F induced pronounced hydrocephalus of the lateral ventricles at 30 days post-infection.
source: Infection with either virus induced pronounced hydrocephalus of the lateral ventricles at 30 dpi (Figure 2A) with multiple foci of ablated ependyma and dysplastic changes in the choroid plexus (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: Infection with either A2 or A2.V296F caused multiple foci of ablated ependyma and dysplastic changes in the choroid plexus at 30 days post-infection.
source: Infection with either virus induced pronounced hydrocephalus of the lateral ventricles at 30 dpi (Figure 2A) with multiple foci of ablated ependyma and dysplastic changes in the choroid plexus (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: Brains of mice infected with either A2 or A2.V296F had an expansion of the vimentin+ region abutting the ventricles at 30 days post-infection.
source: Brains of mice infected with either virus had an expansion of the vimentin+ region abutting the ventricles, indicating damage to and/or disruption of the ependymal lining as a result of infection (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2D

claim: The ependyma and periventricular region had aggregates of CD3+ T cells in both A2- and A2.V296F-infected mice at 30 days post-infection.
source: The ependyma and periventricular region had aggregates of CD3+ T cells and were diffusely infiltrated by Iba1+ cells (macrophages or microglia) in both A2- and A2.V296F-infected mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The ependyma and periventricular region were diffusely infiltrated by Iba1+ cells (macrophages or microglia) in both A2- and A2.V296F-infected mice at 30 days post-infection.
source: The ependyma and periventricular region had aggregates of CD3+ T cells and were diffusely infiltrated by Iba1+ cells (macrophages or microglia) in both A2- and A2.V296F-infected mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Incubation of MuPyV with 8A7H5 prior to infection potently neutralized A2 but did not affect infectivity by A2.V296F.
source: Incubation of MuPyV with 8A7H5 prior to infection potently neutralized A2 but did not affect infectivity by A2.V296F.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the manuscript text

claim: Replacement of V296 with alanine or isoleucine did not abrogate neutralization by 8A7H5.
source: Replacement of V296 with alanine or isoleucine did not abrogate neutralization by 8A7H5, but substitution to tyrosine or tryptophan also conferred resistance to neutralization (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Substitution of V296 to tyrosine or tryptophan conferred resistance to neutralization by 8A7H5.
source: Replacement of V296 with alanine or isoleucine did not abrogate neutralization by 8A7H5, but substitution to tyrosine or tryptophan also conferred resistance to neutralization (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Spread of A2 infection in mouse fibroblast monolayers was significantly impaired by 8A7H5.
source: Spread of A2 infection in mouse fibroblast monolayers was significantly impaired by 8A7H5, but spread by A2.V296F was unimpeded (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Spread of A2.V296F infection in mouse fibroblast monolayers was unimpeded by 8A7H5.
source: Spread of A2 infection in mouse fibroblast monolayers was significantly impaired by 8A7H5, but spread by A2.V296F was unimpeded (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: 8A7H5 immunization resulted in undetectable splenic LT mRNA levels in A2-infected mice 4 days post-infection.
source: 8A7H5 immunization resulted in undetectable splenic LT mRNA levels in A2-infected mice 4 dpi, but had no effect on virus levels in A2.V296F-infected mice (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: 8A7H5 immunization had no effect on virus levels in A2.V296F-infected mice 4 days post-infection.
source: 8A7H5 immunization resulted in undetectable splenic LT mRNA levels in A2-infected mice 4 dpi, but had no effect on virus levels in A2.V296F-infected mice (Figure 3D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: 8A7H5 was able to prevent binding of over 80% of MuPyV-specific IgG to VP1 pentamers.
source: Notably, we found that the IgG response to A2 MuPyV infection in WT mice competed with 8A7H5 for attachment to VP1, with 8A7H5 able to prevent binding of over 80% of MuPyV-specific IgG to VP1 pentamers (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Refinement of cryo-EM datasets produced maps at 3.9 Å and 4.2 Å resolution for the A2 and A2-Fab complex, respectively.
source: Refinement of both datasets produced maps at 3.9 Å and 4.2 Å resolution for the A2 and A2-Fab complex, respectively (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 2; Punjani et al., 2017; Zivanov et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 2

claim: The complex map revealed 360 epitopes were possible for 8A7H5 Fab, corresponding to six copies per asymmetric unit.
source: In contrast to the 60 epitopes present in the BKPyV:scFv structure (one per asymmetric unit), our complex map revealed 360 epitopes were possible for 8A7H5 Fab, corresponding to six copies per asymmetric unit; that is, 1 Fab may bind each VP1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Lindner et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citation to Lindner et al., 2019

claim: Sub-particle refinement improved the resolution of the pentavalent and hexavalent capsomers for both the A2 and A2-Fab complex to 2.9 and 3.2 Å, respectively.
source: Sub-particle refinement improved the resolution of the pentavalent and hexavalent capsomers for both the A2 and A2-Fab complex (2.9 and 3.2 Å, respectively) (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E

claim: The refinement improved the resolution of the virus–Fab interface to 3.1–3.3 Å, with sidechain density clearly apparent.
source: This refinement also improved the resolution of the virus–Fab interface to 3.1–3.3 Å, with sidechain density clearly apparent (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 5

claim: The six epitopes in the asymmetric unit superimposed with a range of C alpha root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.40 Å to 0.51 Å.
source: After refining the build independently into each corresponding map density, loops comprising the six distinct epitopes in the asymmetric unit superimposed with a range of C alpha root mean square deviation (RMSD) of 0.40 Å to 0.51 Å.
evidence: Stated as a finding from structural analysis

claim: The 8A7H5 epitope consisted of thirteen residues of the BC and HI loops of VP1, and three residues from the DE (141, 151) and HI (292) loops of the adjacent VP1.
source: On the virus capsid the 8A7H5 epitope consisted of thirteen residues of the BC and HI loops of VP1, and three residues from the DE (141, 151) and HI (292) loops of the adjacent VP1 (Table 1, Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 1, Figure 5A and B

claim: There was a predicted salt-bridge between VP1 R77 and D99 located in CDR loop H3 of 8A7H5.
source: There was a predicted salt-bridge between VP1 R77 and D99 located in CDR loop H3 of 8A7H5 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: The 8A7H5 epitope overlapped with residues associated with receptor binding.
source: The 8A7H5 epitope overlapped with residues associated with receptor binding (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: 8A7H5 mAb blocked A2 viral attachment but had no effect on A2.V296F attachment.
source: 8A7H5 mAb/Fab blocked A2 viral attachment, but had no effect on A2.V296F attachment as assayed by flow cytometry (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The V296F mutation placed a bulky phenylalanine sidechain directly within the Fab-virus interface likely disrupting the interaction with the CDR loop H3 through steric hindrance.
source: The V296F mutation placed a bulky phenylalanine sidechain directly within the Fab-virus interface likely disrupting the interaction with the CDR loop H3 through steric hindrance (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5F

claim: There was a significant reduction in 8A7H5 binding to A2.V296F compared to A2.
source: Consistent with this model, direct binding assays showed a significant reduction in 8A7H5 binding to A2.V296F compared to A2 (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: There was no steric clash observed between Fabs bound to neighboring epitopes.
source: Surprisingly, there was no steric clash observed between Fabs bound to neighboring epitopes (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The MuPyV capsid was able to accommodate 360 copies of 8A7H5 Fab, saturating all available epitopes.
source: This observation indicates that the MuPyV capsid was able to accommodate 360 copies of 8A7H5 Fab, saturating all available epitopes.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis

claim: All mutant viruses (A2.V296F, A2.V296Y, A2.N293F, A2.N293Y) showed a defect in kidney infection following subcutaneous inoculation.
source: All mutant viruses showed a defect in kidney infection following s.c. inoculation, similar to A2.V296F (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Inoculation intracranially with mutant viruses (A2.V296F, A2.V296Y, A2.N293F, A2.N293Y) resulted in similar levels of infection in the brain compared to A2.
source: Inoculation i.c. with these viruses resulted in similar levels of infection in the brain compared to A2 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: A2.V296Y conferred complete resistance to 8A7H5.
source: Predictably, V296Y conferred complete resistance to 8A7H5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: A2.N293F and A2.N293Y remained sensitive to 8A7H5 neutralization.
source: A2.N293F and A2.N293Y remained sensitive to 8A7H5 neutralization (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: 8A7H5 showed high avidity interactions with WT and N293Y VP1 pentamers.
source: 8A7H5 showed high avidity interactions with WT and N293Y VP1 pentamers, and low avidity with V296F pentamers.
evidence: Stated as a finding from avidity measurements

claim: 8A7H5 showed low avidity with V296F pentamers.
source: 8A7H5 showed high avidity interactions with WT and N293Y VP1 pentamers, and low avidity with V296F pentamers.
evidence: Stated as a finding from avidity measurements

claim: The R77N and H139R mutations each reduced 8A7H5 avidity to a similar extent as V296F.
source: The R77N and H139R mutations each reduced 8A7H5 avidity to a similar extent as V296F, suggesting that these mutations would also confer resistance to 8A7H5.
evidence: Stated as a finding from avidity measurements

claim: The T291D mutation decreased 8A7H5 avidity, but not to the extent of R77N, H139R, and V296F.
source: The T291D mutation also decreased 8A7H5 avidity, but not to the extent of R77N, H139R, and V296F (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Three VP1 mutant viruses were isolated from serial passage of A2 in the presence of 8A7H5: an N80K point mutation and two single amino acid deletions, ∆294 and ∆295.
source: Three VP1 mutant viruses were isolated, an N80K point mutation in the VP1 BC loop and two single amino acid deletions, ∆294 and ∆295, adjacent to V296F in the HI loop.
evidence: Stated as a finding from serial passage experiments

claim: The N80K, ∆294, and ∆295 mutations each conferred complete resistance to 8A7H5-mediated neutralization.
source: These mutations each conferred complete resistance to 8A7H5-mediated neutralization (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: Infection of mice subcutaneously with A2.∆294 resulted in elevated virus levels in the kidney.
source: Infection of mice s.c. with the mutant viruses resulted in elevated virus levels of A2.∆294 and reduced virus levels of A2.N80K and A2.∆295 in the kidney, indicating that these mutations have varying effects on kidney tropism (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: Infection of mice subcutaneously with A2.N80K and A2.∆295 resulted in reduced virus levels in the kidney.
source: Infection of mice s.c. with the mutant viruses resulted in elevated virus levels of A2.∆294 and reduced virus levels of A2.N80K and A2.∆295 in the kidney, indicating that these mutations have varying effects on kidney tropism (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: All three mutant viruses (A2.N80K, A2.∆294, A2.∆295) had reduced brain infection levels following intracranial inoculation compared to A2.
source: All three mutant viruses had reduced brain infection levels following i.c. inoculation compared to A2 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: At 14 days post-infection, virus shed in the urine of μMT mice was heavily biased towards A2, despite the mice having high levels of A2.V296F in the blood and brain tissue.
source: At 14 dpi, virus shed in the urine was heavily biased towards A2, despite the mice having high levels of A2.V296F in the blood and brain tissue (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: A severe impediment to kidney replication limits shedding of the V296F mutant virus in the urine, despite being viremic.
source: This result showed that a severe impediment to kidney replication limits shedding of the V296F mutant virus in the urine, despite being viremic.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data in Figure 6I

claim: VP1 mutations in polyomaviruses concomitantly enabled evasion of the nAb response and facilitated neurovirulence by preserving viral replication in the CNS.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that VP1 mutations in polyomaviruses concomitantly enabled evasion of the nAb response and facilitated neurovirulence by preserving viral replication in the CNS.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings

claim: Viremia by nAb-resistant VP1 JCPyV variants is a critical early step in PML pathogenesis.
source: These findings support the concept that viremia by nAb-resistant VP1 JCPyV variants is a critical early step in PML pathogenesis.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings

claim: The main contact residues of the Fab mapped to the heavy chain with minor contributions from the light chain.
source: The main contact residues of the Fab mapped to the heavy chain with minor contributions from the light chain (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Stated as a finding from structural analysis

claim: The heavy chain made all contacts with one copy of the coat protein, whereas the light chain interacted with the adjacent VP1.
source: The heavy chain made all contacts with one copy of the coat protein, whereas the light chain interacted with the adjacent VP1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The mechanism of antibody neutralization is to block the receptor-binding site and prevent virus interaction with the host cell.
source: This overlap suggests that the mechanism of antibody neutralization is to block the receptor-binding site and prevent virus interaction with the host cell.
evidence: Inferred from structural overlap between epitope and receptor-binding site

claim: Loss of antibody binding to R77N pentamers is probably due to the lost salt-bridge between VP1 R77 and D99 in CDR loop H3 of 8A7H5.
source: Loss of antibody binding to R77N pentamers is probably due to the lost salt-bridge between VP1 R77 and D99 in CDR loop H3 of 8A7H5.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis

claim: Deletion of contact residue Y294 or the immediately adjacent D295 provide escape through shortening and reorganization of the key antigenic HI loop.
source: Deletion of contact residue Y294 or the immediately adjacent D295 provide escape through shortening and reorganization of the key antigenic HI loop.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis

claim: The N80K substitution would disrupt the interaction with 8A7H5 by introducing a positive charge and a longer sidechain.
source: The N80K substitution would disrupt this interaction by introducing a positive charge and a longer sidechain.
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis

claim: 8A7H5 binding may stabilize the virus and prevent uncoating.
source: Because the 8A7H5 epitope bridges neighboring VP1 molecules within each capsomer, 8A7H5 binding may stabilize the virus and prevent uncoating.
evidence: Speculated based on structural analysis

claim: The salt-bridge formed between the R77 of VP1 on the virus and antibody residue D99 mimics the essential interaction of R77 with the sialic acid moiety of the host cell receptor.
source: The salt-bridge formed between the R77 of VP1 on the virus and antibody residue D99 mimics the essential interaction of R77 with the sialic acid moiety of the host cell receptor (Bauer et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 1999

claim: Loss of kidney tropism and retained brain tropism by VP1 mutant viruses may be explained by differences in host cell receptor expression between these organs.
source: Loss of kidney tropism and retained brain tropism by VP1 mutant viruses may be explained by differences in host cell receptor expression between these organs.
evidence: Speculated based on experimental findings

claim: Mutations in solvent-exposed VP1 loops could skew binding to a decoy receptor selectively expressed in the kidney that diverts virions to a nonproductive infection pathway.
source: Mutations in solvent-exposed VP1 loops could skew binding to a decoy receptor selectively expressed in the kidney that diverts virions to a nonproductive infection pathway.
evidence: Speculated based on experimental findings

claim: VP1 mutations could attenuate or even negate binding to receptor(s) necessary for kidney infection, whereas a different receptor(s) is (are) expressed in the CNS.
source: Alternatively, VP1 mutations could attenuate or even negate binding to receptor(s) necessary for kidney infection, whereas a different receptor(s) is (are) expressed in the CNS.
evidence: Speculated based on experimental findings

claim: WT JCPyV can bind both sialyated glycans and non-sialylated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), whereas JCPyV-PML VP1 mutants only bind GAGs.
source: Supporting this possibility is recent evidence showing that WT JCPyV can bind both sialyated glycans and non-sialylated glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), whereas JCPyV-PML VP1 mutants only bind GAGs (Geoghegan et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geoghegan et al., 2017

claim: Emergence of VP1 mutant JCPyVs in PML patients but not healthy individuals infers that viruses with these mutations have a replication advantage in the setting of depressed immune status.
source: Emergence of VP1 mutant JCPyVs in PML patients but not healthy individuals infers that viruses with these mutations have a replication advantage in the setting of depressed immune status (Zheng et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2005

claim: Mutations in the four receptor-binding loops of VP1 are typically detrimental to viral fitness and persistence.
source: Mutations in the four receptor-binding loops of VP1 are typically detrimental to viral fitness and persistence (Bauer et al., 1999; Caruso et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bauer et al., 1999; Caruso et al., 2003

claim: Evasion of host antibodies provides a strong selective pressure to promote the spread of an otherwise replication-disadvantageous mutation.
source: Evasion of host antibodies provides a strong selective pressure to promote the spread of an otherwise replication-disadvantageous mutation.
evidence: Stated as an inference from experimental findings

claim: The mutant A2.V296F virus strongly outcompeted parental A2 virus in the blood and brain, but was still poorly shed into the urine, when faced with an A2-nAb.
source: Experimental demonstration of this scenario comes from evidence that the mutant A2.V296F virus strongly outcompeted parental A2 virus in the blood and brain, but was still poorly shed into the urine, when faced with an A2-nAb (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: Selection of VP1 mutants is driven by an antibody response sufficient to control parental but not a VP1 mutant virus.
source: Our data agree with recent reports showing poor neutralization by sera from PML patients for their VP1 mutant JCPyVs, and indicate that selection of VP1 mutants is driven by an antibody response sufficient to control parental but not a VP1 mutant virus (Jelcic et al., 2015; Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jelcic et al., 2015; Ray et al., 2015 and experimental data

claim: JCPyV takes a hit to viral fitness in order to evade humoral immunity.
source: Thus, our findings indicate that JCPyV takes a hit to viral fitness in order to evade humoral immunity.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings

claim: Antibody escape is a requisite first step in PML development.
source: By extension, our results strongly support the concept that antibody escape is a requisite first step in PML development.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings

claim: JCPyV viremia is found in multiple sclerosis patients treated with natalizumab.
source: JCPyV viremia is found in multiple sclerosis patients treated with natalizumab (Major et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Major et al., 2013

claim: JCPyV infects primary choroid plexus epithelial cells.
source: In support of a choroid plexus-mediated route, JCPyV infects primary choroid plexus epithelial cells, and JCPyV-infected choroid plexi are found in PML brains (Corbridge et al., 2019; O'Hara et al., 2020; O'Hara et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corbridge et al., 2019; O'Hara et al., 2020; O'Hara et al., 2018

claim: JCPyV-infected choroid plexi are found in PML brains.
source: In support of a choroid plexus-mediated route, JCPyV infects primary choroid plexus epithelial cells, and JCPyV-infected choroid plexi are found in PML brains (Corbridge et al., 2019; O'Hara et al., 2020; O'Hara et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Corbridge et al., 2019; O'Hara et al., 2020; O'Hara et al., 2018

claim: Both A2 and A2.V296F viruses productively infect the ependyma.
source: Both A2 and A2.V296F viruses productively infect the ependyma, and we reported ependymal infection by MuPyV under conditions of immune suppression (Mockus et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mockus et al., 2020

claim: Ventricular enlargement has been reported late in the course of PML disease and in a case of JCPyV meningitis.
source: Ventricular enlargement has been reported late in the course of PML disease and in a case of JCPyV meningitis (Agnihotri et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agnihotri et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2015

claim: Evasion of the nAb response is the dominant driver of VP1 mutant viruses that retain CNS tropism.
source: Using the MuPyV CNS infection model, we demonstrate that evasion of the host's neutralizing antiviral humoral response is the dominant driver of VP1 mutant viruses that retain CNS tropism.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings

claim: VP1 mutations do not act per se to render JCPyV neurovirulent.
source: Our findings argue against the concept that VP1 mutations act per se to render JCPyV neurovirulent.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings

claim: Viremia, consequent to outgrowth of antibody-escape VP1 variants, is a critical step in PML pathogenesis.
source: Instead our work supports the model that viremia, consequent to outgrowth of antibody-escape VP1 variants, is a critical step in PML pathogenesis.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the study findings
